TraceWin agent benchmark -- results and commentary¶

This notebook does not run TraceWin or train policies. It loads and comments the artifacts already saved under results/benchmark and results/train/rl.

The headline result is now final_thesis_031_a015_s025_steps300k_tracewin.json: seven policies, each evaluated over 20 matched-reset episodes (maximum 20 steps) in the real TraceWin environment on the 18-parameter ADIGE configuration. Section 0 shows the complete result and compares it directly with the preceding dataset 018; section 0b reports the workspace-2 evaluation with episodes extended to 30 steps.

Sections 1-6 retain the detailed dataset-018 campaign as historical context; section 7 covers the older surrogate-environment artifact, section 8 contains the takeaways, and section 9 closes with the operational timing comparison. For generating new numbers, use tracewin_agents_benchmark.ipynb, which actually drives TraceWin.

def find_repository_root(start=Path.cwd()):

0. Dataset 031: result and comparison with dataset 018¶

Both artifacts use the same score implementation and the same 20 reset indices for every policy, so the per-episode comparison below is paired. A failure is an episode whose final score equals ERROR_SCORE = -999. The confidence intervals are bootstrap intervals of the paired mean difference $\mathrm{score}_{031}-\mathrm{score}_{018}$.

In [2]:
benchmark_031_path = BENCHMARK_DIR / "final_thesis_031_a015_s025_steps300k_tracewin.json"
benchmark_018_path = BENCHMARK_DIR / "final_thesis_018_a015_s025_steps300k_tracewin.json"

benchmark_031 = json.loads(benchmark_031_path.read_text())
benchmark_018 = json.loads(benchmark_018_path.read_text())
tracewin_031 = benchmark_031["policy_evaluation_tracewin"]
tracewin_018 = benchmark_018["policy_evaluation_tracewin"]
error_score_031 = float(benchmark_031["score_function"]["error_score"])

assert benchmark_031["score_function"]["sha256"] == benchmark_018["score_function"]["sha256"]

def canonical_episodes(tracewin):
    frame = pd.DataFrame(tracewin["episodes"]).copy()
    frame["algorithm"] = frame["algorithm"].map(display_name)
    return frame

episodes_031 = canonical_episodes(tracewin_031)
episodes_018 = canonical_episodes(tracewin_018)

def compact_summary(tracewin, episodes, error_score):
    raw = pd.DataFrame(tracewin["summary"]).T.copy()
    raw.index = raw.index.map(display_name)
    failures = episodes.groupby("algorithm")["final_score"].apply(
        lambda values: int(np.isclose(values, error_score).sum())
    )
    medians = episodes.groupby("algorithm")["final_score"].median()
    result = pd.DataFrame({
        "episodes": raw["episodes"].astype(int),
        "score mean": raw["final_score_mean"],
        "score std": raw["final_score_std"],
        "score median": medians,
        "mean npart ratio": raw["final_npart_ratio_mean"],
        "failures": failures,
        "failure rate": failures / raw["episodes"],
        "best observed score": raw["best_observed_score"],
    })
    return result.sort_values("score mean", ascending=False)

summary_031 = compact_summary(tracewin_031, episodes_031, error_score_031)
summary_018 = compact_summary(tracewin_018, episodes_018, error_score_031)

display(Markdown("### Complete dataset-031 ranking"))
display(summary_031.style.format({
    "score mean": "{:.2f}", "score std": "{:.2f}",
    "score median": "{:.2f}", "mean npart ratio": "{:.3f}",
    "failure rate": "{:.0%}", "best observed score": "{:.2f}",
}).background_gradient(subset=["score mean"], cmap="RdYlGn"))

paired_031 = episodes_031.pivot(index="episode", columns="algorithm", values="final_score")
paired_018 = episodes_018.pivot(index="episode", columns="algorithm", values="final_score")
algorithms = sorted(set(paired_031.columns) & set(paired_018.columns))

bootstrap_rows = []
bootstrap_samples = 20_000
for offset, algorithm in enumerate(algorithms):
    delta = (paired_031[algorithm] - paired_018[algorithm]).dropna().to_numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(20260822 + offset)
    draws = delta[rng.integers(0, len(delta), size=(bootstrap_samples, len(delta)))].mean(axis=1)
    low, high = np.quantile(draws, [0.025, 0.975])
    bootstrap_rows.append({
        "algorithm": algorithm, "paired delta": delta.mean(),
        "CI low": low, "CI high": high,
        "paired win rate": np.mean(delta > 0),
    })
paired_stats = pd.DataFrame(bootstrap_rows).set_index("algorithm")

comparison = pd.DataFrame(index=algorithms)
comparison["mean 018"] = summary_018.loc[algorithms, "score mean"]
comparison["mean 031"] = summary_031.loc[algorithms, "score mean"]
comparison["delta mean"] = comparison["mean 031"] - comparison["mean 018"]
comparison["failures 018"] = summary_018.loc[algorithms, "failures"].astype(int)
comparison["failures 031"] = summary_031.loc[algorithms, "failures"].astype(int)
comparison["mean npart 018"] = summary_018.loc[algorithms, "mean npart ratio"]
comparison["mean npart 031"] = summary_031.loc[algorithms, "mean npart ratio"]
comparison = comparison.join(paired_stats)
comparison = comparison.sort_values("delta mean", ascending=False)

display(Markdown("### Dataset 031 minus dataset 018"))
display(comparison.style.format({
    "mean 018": "{:.2f}", "mean 031": "{:.2f}",
    "delta mean": "{:+.2f}", "paired delta": "{:+.2f}",
    "CI low": "{:+.2f}", "CI high": "{:+.2f}",
    "paired win rate": "{:.0%}",
    "mean npart 018": "{:.3f}", "mean npart 031": "{:.3f}",
}).background_gradient(subset=["delta mean"], cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-50, vmax=50))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.2))

ranking = summary_031.sort_values("score mean")
axes[0].barh(
    ranking.index, ranking["score mean"], xerr=ranking["score std"],
    color="#4c78a8", alpha=0.85, capsize=3,
)
axes[0].axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set_title("Dataset 031: final score (mean ± std)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Final score")
axes[0].grid(axis="x")
axes[0].grid(False, axis="y")

deltas = comparison.sort_values("paired delta")
xerr = np.vstack([
    deltas["paired delta"] - deltas["CI low"],
    deltas["CI high"] - deltas["paired delta"],
])
axes[1].errorbar(
    deltas["paired delta"], deltas.index, xerr=xerr,
    fmt="o", color="#4c78a8", ecolor="#777777", capsize=4,
)
axes[1].axvline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.9)
axes[1].set_title("Dataset 031 − 018 (paired 95% bootstrap CI)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Mean final-score change")
axes[1].grid(axis="x")
axes[1].grid(False, axis="y")

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Assessment¶

Dataset 031 is better in its strongest result, but not uniformly better:

  • svg_final is the clearest improvement: its mean rises from about $-106.37$ to $51.07$, and its failures fall from 3/20 to 0/20. It is now the best policy by mean score. The paired bootstrap interval is just above zero, so this is the only clearly supported mean improvement.
  • td3, sac, svg_uniform, and svg_final form a robust top group in dataset 031: all have zero failures, means between roughly 43 and 51, and standard deviations around 9-10. td3 and svg_uniform improve slightly relative to 018, while sac is essentially unchanged.
  • ppo is essentially unchanged and still has one failure. a2c remains unreliable with 14/20 failures. ddpg gets worse because dataset 031 contains one terminal failure, which pulls its mean down sharply.

So the practical answer is: 031 is preferable if the target policy is svg_final, and its high-performing group looks sound, but the benchmark does not support saying that dataset 031 improves every RL algorithm.

0b. Dataset 031: workspace 2 benchmark with 30-step episodes¶

This is the benchmark stored in final_thesis_031_a015_s025_steps300k_workspace2_30steps: the same seven policies are evaluated for 20 episodes each on real TraceWin, with a maximum trajectory length of 30 steps. The comparison with the 20-step result below is descriptive; extending an episode changes the states visited and can create both additional improvement opportunities and additional chances of losing the beam.

30-step assessment¶

The longer evaluation strengthens the reliable top group. td3 ranks first with a mean final score of 58.01, followed by svg_final at 55.23; both have zero failures and substantially smaller dispersion than in the 20-step evaluation. sac also improves to 49.32, while svg_uniform remains broadly stable at 44.91.

The extra ten steps hurt the already unstable policies: ppo and ddpg each move from one to two failures, and a2c from 14 to 15. Their strongly negative means are therefore dominated by terminal beam-loss episodes. Overall, 30 steps make the separation between robust and fragile policies clearer; among the robust policies, td3 has the strongest final-state result in this run.

1. Training run and learning curves¶

The seven policies benchmarked in the following sections come from final_thesis_018_a015_s025_steps300k. The model-free agents were trained for 300,000 environment steps on the surrogate; the SVG curves use their own episode-based budget and therefore end earlier on the common step axis. Every run used three seeds (42, 43, 44) and the same reward regularization:

reward = score / 100
       - 0.02 * distance_penalty
       - 0.15 * action_penalty
       - 0.25 * action_smoothness_penalty
       - 5.00 * score_regression_penalty

The solid line is the mean evaluation score across seeds and the shaded band shows their dispersion. These evaluations are performed on the surrogate: they measure optimization and convergence during training, whereas sections 3-6 measure transfer and reliability on real TraceWin.

Aggregate learning curves (three training seeds)

The training curves separate two questions that the benchmark alone cannot. svg_uniform and svg_final optimize the surrogate quickly, while sac improves more slowly and stabilizes only in the latter part of training. td3 also reaches a stable high plateau; a2c and ddpg remain much noisier and lower. The TraceWin columns show why training score is not sufficient for model selection: svg_final looks strong on the surrogate but transfers unreliably, whereas td3, sac and svg_uniform retain good final performance on TraceWin. The two score columns deliberately are not subtracted: one is a best surrogate-validation statistic and the other is a mean final real-machine score, so their numerical difference would not be a like-for-like estimate of the sim-to-real gap.

2. Score function and run configuration¶

Every artifact in this folder embeds the same score_function metadata, so loading it once is enough to interpret every table and plot below. The score is ERROR_SCORE = -999 whenever the beam is fully lost (npart_ratio <= 0); otherwise it is a weighted, linear combination of the transmitted-particle fraction and penalties on emittance, beam offset, angle and size, each measured against a reference value.

3. Final-policy comparison (7 agents plus bayesian)¶

final_score_mean/_std describe the state the episode actually ends in -- the number that matters operationally, since that is the configuration a policy would actually leave the machine in. best_observed_score is a different, more optimistic number: the highest score seen at any reset or step, even if the policy immediately moved away from it again (more on that gap below). Because every algorithm uses the same episode seeds, comparisons can also be made pairwise on identical starting conditions.

bayesian: warm-started TraceWin optimization reference¶

bayesian is the completed campaign under warm_start_workspace1_5x300: five independent Gaussian-Process runs, each with 300 new evaluations performed directly in TraceWin. The optimizers were initialized from 46 valid configurations selected from the existing dataset.

The reported value is the best selected configuration among 1,500 new TraceWin evaluations, not a mean over 20 matched-reset episodes. It is therefore shown as a classical optimization reference, but is deliberately not inserted into the agents' mean/std ranking. This campaign and the policy benchmark store the same score-function hash.

In [7]:
bayesian_path = BAYESIAN_DIR / "results.json"
bayesian_report = json.loads(bayesian_path.read_text())
bayesian_evaluations = [
    evaluation
    for run in bayesian_report["runs"]
    for evaluation in run["evaluations"]
]
bayesian_best = bayesian_report["best_result"]
bayesian_default = bayesian_report.get("default_result") or {}

assert bayesian_report["score_function"]["sha256"] == final_thesis["score_function"]["sha256"]

bayesian_reference_df = pd.DataFrame([{
    "runs": len(bayesian_report["runs"]),
    "evaluations/run": bayesian_report["config"]["n_calls"],
    "total evaluations": len(bayesian_evaluations),
    "successful": sum(bool(row.get("success")) for row in bayesian_evaluations),
    "failed": sum(not bool(row.get("success")) for row in bayesian_evaluations),
    "warm-start points": len(bayesian_report.get("warm_start", [])),
    "best score": bayesian_best["score"],
    "best run": int(bayesian_best["run_index"]) + 1,
    "best call": int(bayesian_best["call_index"]) + 1,
    "default score": bayesian_default.get("score") if bayesian_default.get("success") else np.nan,
    "bounds scale": bayesian_report["config"]["bounds_scale"],
}]).T.rename(columns={0: "value"})
display(bayesian_reference_df.style.format({"value": lambda value: f"{value:,.3f}" if isinstance(value, float) else f"{value:,}"}))

The five curves below show the incumbent best score within each independent 300-evaluation run. All runs converge to a narrow range (59.35--60.36); the global best is 60.359, found by run 5 at its 183rd new TraceWin evaluation. The second plot expresses the best configuration's displacement from the nominal machine settings in parameter-sensitivity units and annotates the physical deltas.

Reading the ranking:

  • td3, sac, svg_uniform form the top cluster: final score in the +40-48 range with the tightest spreads (std ~10), and the best transmitted fractions (final_npart_ratio_mean ~0.42-0.49). These are the three policies that reliably leave the machine in a good state.
  • ddpg lands close to zero mean score with a comparatively large std -- it neither fails outright nor consistently finds a good configuration.
  • ppo and svg_final (stored as svg_finale in this legacy artifact) have slightly negative mean scores with very large std (225 and 375). A negative mean next to a competitive best_observed_score (61.3 and 63.4, both near the top of the whole table) is the signature of a policy that can reach good states but does not do so reliably -- section 4 quantifies this with an explicit failure rate.
  • a2c is the outlier: mean final score of -698 with std 460, i.e. most episodes end near ERROR_SCORE = -999 (total particle loss).

Both figures share four panels -- final_score, final_emittance, final_npart_ratio, total_reward (the RL reward accumulated over the episode, on its own bounded scale, not the physical score). The box plot is the more informative of the two here: the circles below each a2c, ppo and svg_final box are individual failed episodes pinned at the -999/0 floor. These failures drag the means down and inflate the error bars; the box plot distinguishes occasional catastrophic outcomes from consistently mediocre performance.

4. Why the error bars are so large: per-episode failure rate¶

A final_score at the -999 floor means npart_ratio <= 0 -- the episode ended with the beam fully lost. Splitting each algorithm's 20 episodes into "reached the floor" vs. "did not" turns the qualitative box-plot reading above into a single reliability number per algorithm.

a2c loses the beam entirely in 70% of its episodes, which by itself explains its −698 mean and 460 std in section 3 -- this is not a noisy policy, it is a mostly-broken one on this checkpoint. svg_final (legacy artifact key: svg_finale, 15%) and ppo (5%) fail occasionally, enough to pull their means below zero despite competitive best-case scores. ddpg, sac, svg_uniform and td3 never lose the beam in this batch of episodes, which is a necessary (if not sufficient) condition for the tight error bars they show in section 3.

5. Statistical robustness and matched-reset comparison¶

Mean ± standard deviation alone is difficult to interpret when a few runs hit the -999 failure floor. The table and thesis-ready figure below add bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, median/IQR, success-conditioned score, Wilson intervals for beam-loss rate, and paired score differences. Pairing is justified because episode i uses the same reset seed for every policy. These intervals describe this 20-reset campaign; they are not guarantees for all possible machine conditions.

In [11]:
BOOTSTRAP_SAMPLES = 20_000
BOOTSTRAP_SEED = 20260804

def bootstrap_mean_ci(values, samples=BOOTSTRAP_SAMPLES, seed=BOOTSTRAP_SEED):
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = rng.choice(values, size=(samples, len(values)), replace=True).mean(axis=1)
    return np.quantile(means, [0.025, 0.975])

def wilson_interval(successes, total, z=1.96):
    p = successes / total
    denominator = 1 + z**2 / total
    centre = (p + z**2 / (2 * total)) / denominator
    margin = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / total + z**2 / (4 * total**2)) / denominator
    return centre - margin, centre + margin

ranking = summary_df["final_score_mean"].sort_values().index.tolist()
paired_scores = episodes_df.pivot(index="episode", columns="algorithm", values="final_score")
reference_algorithm = summary_df["final_score_mean"].idxmax()
rows = []
for offset, algorithm in enumerate(ranking):
    values = episodes_df.loc[episodes_df.algorithm == algorithm, "final_score"].to_numpy(float)
    survived = values[values > ERROR_SCORE]
    failed = int((values <= ERROR_SCORE).sum())
    mean_lo, mean_hi = bootstrap_mean_ci(values, seed=BOOTSTRAP_SEED + offset)
    success_lo, success_hi = bootstrap_mean_ci(survived, seed=BOOTSTRAP_SEED + 200 + offset) if len(survived) else (np.nan, np.nan)
    fail_lo, fail_hi = wilson_interval(failed, len(values))
    paired_delta = (paired_scores[algorithm] - paired_scores[reference_algorithm]).to_numpy(float)
    delta_lo, delta_hi = bootstrap_mean_ci(paired_delta, seed=BOOTSTRAP_SEED + 100 + offset)
    rows.append({
        "algorithm": display_name(algorithm),
        "mean_score": values.mean(),
        "mean_ci95_low": mean_lo,
        "mean_ci95_high": mean_hi,
        "median_score": np.median(values),
        "q1_score": np.quantile(values, 0.25),
        "q3_score": np.quantile(values, 0.75),
        "iqr": np.quantile(values, 0.75) - np.quantile(values, 0.25),
        "mean_if_beam_survives": survived.mean() if len(survived) else np.nan,
        "survival_mean_ci95_low": success_lo,
        "survival_mean_ci95_high": success_hi,
        "failed_episodes": failed,
        "failure_rate": failed / len(values),
        "failure_ci95_low": fail_lo,
        "failure_ci95_high": fail_hi,
        f"paired_delta_vs_{display_name(reference_algorithm)}": paired_delta.mean(),
        "paired_delta_ci95_low": delta_lo,
        "paired_delta_ci95_high": delta_hi,
        "paired_win_rate": (paired_delta > 0).mean(),
    })

robust_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("algorithm").sort_values("mean_score", ascending=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Matched-reset reference:** `{display_name(reference_algorithm)}` (highest mean final score)"))
display(robust_df.round(3))

y = np.arange(len(labels))
palette = dict(zip(sorted(robust_df.index), plt.get_cmap("tab10").colors))
colors = [palette[label] for label in labels]

def horizontal_intervals(axis, centres, lows, highs):
    for yi, centre, low, high, color in zip(y, centres, lows, highs, colors):
        axis.errorbar(centre, yi, xerr=[[centre - low], [high - centre]],
                      fmt="none", ecolor=color, capsize=3)

6. Best-observed configuration vs. final-policy performance¶

best_observed_score is the maximum physical score seen at any reset or step of any episode, together with the complete 18-parameter machine configuration that produced it (best_observed_params). gain_over_final_mean is simply best_observed_score - final_score_mean: a large gain means the policy visits a good configuration during the episode but does not end there -- either it keeps exploring past the optimum, or (per section 4) it sometimes loses the beam later in the same trajectory.

    for algo, values in tw["summary"].items()
]

svg_final (gain ~170), a2c (~731) and ppo (~77) show the largest gaps -- consistent with section 4, these are the same three policies with non-zero failure rates: the average is dragged down by episodes that visit a good state and then lose the beam anyway. sac, td3 and svg_uniform have the smallest gains (13-17), meaning their final state is already close to the best state they ever see -- a much more useful property operationally than a high best-case score alone.

Raw absolute deviations are misleading here: solenoid/steerer parameters live around 0.1-0.4 while the electromagnet-lens parameters (AD.EM.*) live in the hundreds to thousands, so an absolute-value table is dominated entirely by the latter. Normalizing each deviation by that parameter's sensitivity (the delta calibrated to move the score by ~1 point) puts all 18 parameters on the same, score-relative scale. On that scale every algorithm's best-observed point sits within roughly half a score-point-equivalent of the nominal ADIGE default on average (0.36-0.68), and no single parameter or algorithm stands out as a qualitatively different regime -- consistent with this being a fine-tuning task around a working machine setup rather than a search for a qualitatively different configuration. ppo has the largest mean deviation (0.68), matching its unstable behavior in sections 3-5; a2c being lowest here is not a sign of good tuning -- most of its "best" points come from very early, near-default resets before the beam is lost.

7. Context: an earlier surrogate-environment benchmark¶

benchmark_policy_summary.csv and benchmark_policy_episodes.csv come from an earlier single-agent run: sb3_sac evaluated over 50 episodes in the fast surrogate environment rather than in TraceWin. The original four-panel plot summarizes final score, final emittance, surviving-particle ratio and cumulative reward as mean ± standard deviation over those 50 episodes. The dashed line in the score panel marks the best result from warm_start_workspace1_5x300 only as a real-TraceWin optimization reference.

This predates the multi-algorithm TraceWin campaign in sections 2-6 and is not on the same footing: different environment, checkpoint, evaluation budget and statistic. It is historical context, not an additional row in the policy ranking.

8. Takeaways¶

  • In the real TraceWin environment, td3, sac and svg_uniform are the most reliable final policies: final score ~40-48, no total-beam-loss episodes in this batch, and the smallest gap between their best-observed and final scores.
  • a2c is effectively broken on this checkpoint (70% total-beam-loss rate); its poor mean score is a reliability problem, not a precision one.
  • ppo and svg_final occasionally reach competitive scores (best-observed near the top of the table) but fail 5-15% of episodes, which is what makes their mean final score negative despite that.
  • ddpg is the middle case: no catastrophic failures, but a final score close to zero -- it survives without particularly optimizing.
  • Every algorithm's best-observed configuration sits close to the nominal ADIGE defaults, confirming this is a fine-tuning task, not a search for a qualitatively different machine setup.
  • The learning curves show that surrogate convergence alone does not guarantee real-machine reliability: svg_final is the clearest counterexample, while td3, sac and svg_uniform combine good training with robust transfer.
  • bayesian found a real-TraceWin score of 60.359 across five independent runs of 300 new evaluations (1,500 total). This is a selected optimum rather than a 20-episode mean, so it is retained as a classical reference rather than ranked as an eighth policy.
  • The surrogate-environment comparison in section 7 is an older artifact, retained only as historical context for a different checkpoint and evaluation protocol.

To generate new numbers instead of reading these, use tracewin_agents_benchmark.ipynb (single checkpoint, real TraceWin) or the benchmark command directly.

9. Timing comparison: one Bayesian run vs one 30-step policy episode¶

This is the operational comparison after model selection. One complete Bayesian run performs 300 new TraceWin evaluations. Deploying the best selected policy (td3 in the workspace-2 30-step benchmark) for one test episode performs at most 30 TraceWin calls: one per environment step. The Bayesian durations are measured from their saved timestamps; the policy duration is estimated explicitly as 30 × mean TraceWin-call time because the benchmark artifact has no timestamps.

In [15]:
from datetime import datetime

def parse_timestamp(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value)

bayesian_timing_rows = []
for run in bayesian_report["runs"]:
    timed = [row for row in run["evaluations"] if row.get("timestamp")]
    timestamps = [parse_timestamp(row["timestamp"]) for row in timed]
    duration_seconds = (max(timestamps) - min(timestamps)).total_seconds()
    bayesian_timing_rows.append({
        "run": int(run["run_index"]) + 1,
        "TraceWin calls": len(timed),
        "failed": sum(not bool(row.get("success")) for row in timed),
        "duration min": duration_seconds / 60,
        "average s/call": duration_seconds / max(1, len(timed) - 1),
        "best score": run["best_score"],
    })

bayesian_timing_df = pd.DataFrame(bayesian_timing_rows).set_index("run")
mean_tracewin_call_seconds = (
    bayesian_timing_df["duration min"].sum() * 60
    / (bayesian_timing_df["TraceWin calls"].sum() - len(bayesian_timing_df))
)
mean_bayesian_run_minutes = bayesian_timing_df["duration min"].mean()
policy_episode_minutes = 30 * mean_tracewin_call_seconds / 60
time_ratio = mean_bayesian_run_minutes / policy_episode_minutes

timing_comparison = pd.DataFrame([
    {"operation": "Best policy: one 30-step test episode",
     "TraceWin calls": 30, "duration min": policy_episode_minutes,
     "timing basis": "estimated: 30 × mean call time"},
    {"operation": "Bayesian Optimization: one complete run",
     "TraceWin calls": 300, "duration min": mean_bayesian_run_minutes,
     "timing basis": "measured mean across 5 runs"},
]).set_index("operation")

display(Markdown("**Measured duration of each Bayesian run**"))
display(bayesian_timing_df.style.format({
    "duration min": "{:.1f}", "average s/call": "{:.1f}",
    "best score": "{:.2f}",
}))
display(Markdown("**Direct timing comparison**"))
display(timing_comparison.style.format({"duration min": "{:.1f}"}))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 5.2))
for run in bayesian_report["runs"]:
    timed = [row for row in run["evaluations"] if row.get("timestamp")]
    timestamps = np.asarray([parse_timestamp(row["timestamp"]) for row in timed])
    scores = np.asarray([row["score"] for row in timed], dtype=float)
    minutes = np.asarray([(timestamp - timestamps.min()).total_seconds() / 60 for timestamp in timestamps])
    order = np.argsort(minutes)
    incumbent = np.maximum.accumulate(scores[order])
    ax.step(minutes[order], incumbent, where="post", linewidth=1.8,
            label=f"Run {int(run['run_index']) + 1} · {minutes[order][-1]:.0f} min")
ax.set_title("Bayesian Optimization convergence against wall-clock time")
ax.set_xlabel("Minutes since the start of each run")
ax.set_ylabel("Best observed score")
ax.grid(alpha=0.35)
ax.legend(ncol=2, loc="lower right", fontsize=8.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Best policy: one 30-step test episode 30 12.2 estimated: 30 × mean call time
Bayesian Optimization: one complete run 300 121.6 measured mean across 5 runs

A TraceWin call takes 24.4 seconds on average in the recorded Bayesian campaign. Consequently, one full 30-step test episode with the already selected best policy is estimated at 12.2 minutes (30 × 24.4 s). One complete Bayesian run uses 300 calls and takes 121.6 minutes on average across the five runs. The Bayesian run therefore costs approximately 10 times more TraceWin calls and wall-clock time than one 30-step policy episode.

The two operations serve different purposes: the Bayesian run searches for one static optimum, whereas the selected policy generates a sequential response for one reset. This deployment comparison excludes policy training, which was already performed offline on the surrogate. Actual elapsed time can change with hardware, cluster load, retries and early episode termination.
